questions.q: Does read access to a parent record (like an Incident) automatically grant access to files attached to it?
options: No — attachments are tracked in their own sys_attachment table, and ACLs there are a separate permission check from the parent record's ACL
Attachment access is controlled exclusively by the attaching user's own role, never by ACLs
Only attachments uploaded by an admin require a separate check
Yes, any user who can read the record can always download any of its attachments
questions.explain: Attachments live in sys_attachment, a separate table from the record they're attached to, and ACLs configured there are evaluated independently of the parent record's own ACL.

questions.q: What real, practical gap does configuring an ACL directly on sys_attachment close?
options: It prevents any attachments from ever being uploaded to a record
A user can have correct read/update access to a record's fields while still being correctly blocked from downloading a more sensitive file attached to that same record
It only affects attachments larger than a certain file size
It removes the need for any ACL on the parent record itself
questions.explain: An attachment ACL lets an agent work a ticket normally while being blocked from a specific sensitive file on it, if that file carries more risk than the ticket's own fields.

questions.q: Is the ability to export a list of records to CSV/Excel automatically granted by read access to those records?
options: Export rights are granted automatically only to admin users
Export is not possible in ServiceNow under any configuration
No — export is governed by its own, separate capability and role requirement, distinct from read access to the underlying records
Yes, any read access to a list automatically includes export rights
questions.explain: Reading records one at a time in the UI and bulk-exporting that same list are governed by distinct capabilities — read access alone doesn't imply export rights.

questions.q: Why does bulk export represent a meaningfully bigger data-leakage risk than viewing records one at a time in the UI?
options: There is no real difference in risk between the two approaches
Bulk export is actually slower than viewing records individually, reducing risk
Exported data leaves the platform's access controls, audit trail, and session boundaries entirely, so it can be moved anywhere outside the organization's control
Exported data is automatically encrypted, making it safer than in-UI viewing
questions.explain: Viewing records in the UI keeps each view inside the platform's own controls; an exported file can be copied, emailed, or carried anywhere once it leaves the platform.

questions.q: What is the practical takeaway for designing attachment and export controls?
options: Assume that granting read access to a table is sufficient to secure both its attachments and its exportability
Treat attachment access and bulk export as their own gated capabilities, not assumptions that follow automatically from a user's read access to records
Only apply export restrictions to tables with fewer than 100 records
Attachment ACLs and export restrictions are redundant with each other and only one is ever needed
questions.explain: Both attachment access and export are separate, distinct gaps from plain record-level read access, and each deserves its own deliberate control.
